opening.headline: When an app container is not connected to a model, this describes how to identify the cause by checking the models declaration in the Compose file and the environment variables being injected.
body: We've launched an AI app in a container, but there are instances where model calls end with connection errors. It's difficult to determine from logs alone whether the model name is incorrect or the address is wrong. If the model address is hardcoded in the code, the same issue recurs every time the environment changes.

In this course, we examine the composition of Compose models, which declare models as services, and the Docker Model Runner that executes models upon receipt. We learn to understand the naming conventions for environment variables injected into applications and to identify the causes of connection failures by examining the configuration.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the configuration of Compose models and Model Runner.
You can find the cause of model connection failure in the Compose settings.

screens.title: The app container is not connected to the model.
screens.lead: Three common symptoms encountered during the process of connecting a model. Selecting each symptom reveals points for consideration.

visual.alt: An arrow from the app container to the model is broken and displays a question mark.

items.prompt: The app container started, but the model call ended with a connection error.
items.answer: The fact that a container is running and the fact that it can be linked to a model are separate issues. The app may not have received the model's address, or the received address may differ from the name the app is reading.

items.prompt: It's difficult to determine whether the model name is incorrect or the address is wrong based on logs alone.
items.answer: The two values are passed via different environment variables, so you must separately verify which one is empty. Knowing which variable name is created in the configuration file makes the direction of log reading clear.

items.prompt: If the model address is fixed in the code, it breaks every time the environment changes.
items.answer: The address for the model varies depending on local, test, or cloud environments. Instead of hardcoding the address in the code, read it from injected environment variables, enabling the same Compose file to be used across multiple environments.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: If a model is declared as a service, how is connection information passed to the app?

screens.title: Preview: Connect local model with app
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: Have you ever run a model locally and connected it to an app?
items.answer: If you've previously run a model locally to connect it with an app, you've likely directly performed three actions: receiving the model, executing it, and providing its address. Compose models automatically handles these three steps by declaring them within a single file.

items.prompt: Where was the model address recorded?
items.answer: Constants, configuration files, and environment variables within the code are common solutions. Constants in the code must be updated when the environment changes, whereas environment variables can provide the values based on the execution environment.

items.prompt: Did the same address work directly across different people's environments?
items.answer: It usually doesn't work. The address varies depending on the environment. Therefore, a structure that separates declaration from address and allows injection is needed, and this structure is verified in the following screen.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the relationship between the Docker Model Runner, which executes the model, and the Compose models that declare it.

screens.title: Docker Model Runner and Compose models
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to walk through the process step by step, from the model being declared and executed to being connected to the app.

visual.alt: Compose file, Docker Model Runner, diagram showing the relationship between app containers.
labels: Docker Hub · OCI Registry · Hugging Face

steps.title: Model Runner runs the model locally after receiving it.
steps.body: The Docker Model Runner enables downloading and running models locally from Docker Hub, OCI-compliant registries, and Hugging Face, and provides consistent handling of the model download and execution process using Docker tools.

steps.title: API that makes it easy to integrate existing apps
steps.body: The model is served via OpenAI-compatible APIs and Ollama-compatible APIs. If your app already uses these APIs, you only need to change the endpoint to connect. This eliminates the need to rebuild your app specifically for the model, which is an advantage.

steps.title: Received when first used, sent when a request comes in
steps.body: The model is downloaded and stored locally the first time it is used. When a request comes in, it loads into memory; when not in use, it is moved back to disk. Since the model can be large, downloading it initially takes time, but after that, it uses the cached model.

steps.title: Declare models next to the service using Compose models
steps.body: In the top-level element of a Compose file named `models`, the app declares the models it requires. By specifying service and model dependencies within a single file, it becomes immediately clear which models are needed, and the responsibility of providing those models can be delegated to the platform.

steps.title: The model field is required.
steps.body: Each model must have a `model` field. The value is an OCI artifact identifier, such as `ai/smollm2`. Compose retrieves this identifier and passes it to the Model Runner for execution.

steps.title: Conditions are required to use it.
steps.body: To use Compose models, a platform must support Docker Compose 2.38 or later or a platform like Docker Model Runner that supports Compose models. The ability to run the same Compose file on different platforms that implement this specification is what defines portability.

screens.outro: We examine in detail the environment variable injection method for connecting the declared model to the app.

screens.title: Environment variable injection: short grammar vs. long grammar
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the two grammars that service references a model, and the environment variables that change accordingly.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the rules by which environment variable names are derived from model names.

tabs.label: Short grammar
tabs.body:
The short syntax lists only the two model names, `llm` and `embedding-model`, under the `app` service's `models`. The top-level `models` entry for `llm` specifies the model to fetch, such as `model: ai/smollm2`. The service's `models` list grants that service access to those models.

The platform automatically creates environment variables from the model names. `llm` produces `LLM_URL` and `LLM_MODEL`; `embedding-model` produces `EMBEDDING_MODEL_URL` and `EMBEDDING_MODEL_MODEL`. The prefix is the uppercase model name, `_URL` is the access address, and `_MODEL` is the model identifier.

tabs.label: Short grammar
tabs.body:
The service stores model names under the `models` key in the format of `endpoint_var` and `model_var`. The name of the environment variable can be set directly.

For example, if `llm` contains `endpoint_var: AI_MODEL_URL` and `model_var: AI_MODEL_NAME`, the service will receive `AI_MODEL_URL` and `AI_MODEL_NAME`. Different names can be assigned to each model, such as providing `EMBEDDING_URL` and `EMBEDDING_NAME` to an embedding model. This approach is used when the app code needs to match the names already read.

tabs.label: If the name is inconsistent
tabs.body:
The app code should read injected environment variables rather than fixed addresses. However, if the app declares reading `AI_MODEL_URL` using a short grammar, the actual variable created is `LLM_URL`. As a result, the variable the app reads becomes empty, leading to a connection failure.

Whether the name is mismatched can be determined by the declaration style. If using a short grammar, compare the variable generated from the model name with the one in the app code. If using a long grammar, compare the name specified in `endpoint_var` with the app code.

tabs.label: Without reference
tabs.body:
The service can only access models explicitly allowed within its `models` item. Even if the top-level `models` declares an `llm`, if the service has no `models` item, the model address will not be injected into the service.

Both a declaration and a reference are required for a variable to be created. When a connection fails, the first thing to verify is the service's `models` reference.

screens.outro: We will now continue by examining the model's own configuration and the provider concept that treats platform features similar to the model as a service.

screens.title: Model configuration and provider service
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Model declarations can include several additional settings. context_size specifies the maximum token context size that the model can handle, and each model has a maximum limit, so hardware considerations require tuning to only the necessary amount. runtime_flags is a list of command-line flags passed directly to the inference engine when starting the model. The --embeddings flag is required when using an embedding model. Platform-specific options are appended using Extension properties starting with "x-". On the other hand, Compose's provider service indicates platform capabilities rather than containers and defines which plugin type is responsible. For example, if the type is "model", it looks for a CLI plugin named "docker-model". Connection information provided by the provider is passed as environment variables to the dependent services, with variable names formed by appending an underscore and the variable name to the service name. For instance, if the service name is "database", it receives a variable such as DATABASE_URL.

terms.tip: This is the maximum token context size of the model. The larger the size, the more resources it consumes, so set it only to the necessary level.
List of command-line flags passed directly to the inference engine without preprocessing.
This is a flag inserted into runtime_flags when using an embedding model.
This attribute is used when a platform implementing a composition specification adds its own proprietary options.
This is a service representing platform functionality, not a container. Its lifecycle is managed by a third-party component, not Compose.
An example of an environment variable where the access address provided by the provider is stored when the service name is database.

screens.outro: Now let's apply what we've seen so far to a single connectivity failure scenario.

screens.title: Explanation: Case of mismatch between model name and endpoint environment variables
screens.lead: This is the instructor walking through the process of diagnosing a compose file that failed to connect. Please follow along by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: A screen displaying a faulty Compose file and a corrected Compose file side by side.
labels: Variables read by the app code: AI_MODEL_URL

steps.title: Read setting and symptoms
steps.body: Service `app` lists only `llm` in `models`, and there is `model: ai/smollm2` in the top-level `models` under `llm`. The app reads the `AI_MODEL_URL` environment variable to connect to the model. The symptom is an error in the app logs indicating that the model address variable is empty.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify the reference to the models of the service
steps.body: First, check if the service references `models`. If no reference exists, no variables will be injected. In this example, `- llm` is present, so there is no issue, and we proceed to the next line.

steps.title: Step 2: Examine the name of the newly created variable.
steps.body: Short grammar creates variable names from model names. Since the model name is `llm`, the generated variables are `LLM_URL` and `LLM_MODEL`. The app reads `AI_MODEL_URL`, which does not match the name. This mismatch is the cause.

steps.title: Step 3: Match the name with a lengthy grammar.
steps.body: Replace the service's `models` with a longer grammar. If `llm` is set with `endpoint_var: AI_MODEL_URL` and `model_var: AI_MODEL_NAME`, the value will be injected as the name read by the app. While you can modify the app code, it's simpler to adjust the settings without touching already deployed code.

steps.title: Step 4: Verify the model values and context size.
steps.body: If it still fails, check that `model` contains a valid identifier. Model Runner cannot fetch a model that does not exist. Also check that `context_size` does not exceed your hardware's capacity.

steps.title: Verification order summary
steps.body: Connection failures should be checked in the following order: missing reference to service `models`, mismatched variable names, model identifier errors. The key point in this case is that even by reading only the configuration file, one can narrow down at which stage the issue arises.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the contents of this class.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: The model declares itself as a service.
screens.lead: This course content is summarized into three aspects: declaration, injection, and verification.

paragraphs: **Declaration**: The model is declared as a service within the top-level `models` element of the Compose file. The OCI artifact identifier is specified in the `model` field, and additional configurations can be set using `context_size` and `runtime_flags` if needed. The task of receiving and running the model is handled by platform components such as Docker Model Runner.

**Injection**: If a service references a model using `models`, the connection address and model name are injected as environment variables. In short syntax, variable names are automatically generated from the model name, while in long syntax, the values are directly specified using `endpoint_var` and `model_var`. Provider services also pass information to environment variables in the same manner.

**Verification**: The app code must read injected variables rather than fixed addresses. If the connection fails, verify the following in order: service reference `models`, variable name match, and model identifier sequence.

glossary.def: This is the top-level element in a Compose file that declares the AI models required by an app.
This is a Docker feature that runs the model locally and provides it via OpenAI-compatible APIs.
This is a lengthy field that directly specifies the environment variable names for the model address and model name injected into the service.
A service representing platform functionality instead of a container. It passes connection information via environment variables.
This is the maximum token context size the model can handle at once.

misconceptions.myth: The model address can be fixed within the code.
misconceptions.fact: The model's address varies depending on the environment. Do not hardcode it in the code; instead, read it from injected environment variables to use the same Compose file across multiple environments.

misconceptions.myth: Once models are declared, all services automatically use the models.
misconceptions.fact: The service must reference the model within its models item for access to be permitted and the variable to be injected.

misconceptions.myth: The larger the context size, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Each model has a maximum context length and hardware constraints. It's best to scale only as much as necessary.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The model declares itself as a service.
Connection information is injected as environment variables.
Variable names must match app code.
Provider services connect platform features in the same way.
